Most people aren't realizing that Epinephrine isn't a patented drug, what is patented is the EpiPen. The EpiPen is super convenient to use, it holds the exact dosage needed, is portable, very easy to use (just ram it into your thigh and hold for 3 seconds), and has a one year life (and actually secretly stays potent for up to 5 months past it's expiration date), new ones even come with an app for your phone to let you know when the EpiPen is outside of it's temperature zone, when you walk too far away from it, and when it expires.

What most people don't realize is that, if you don't want to pay hundreds of dollars for one, you can ask you doctor for a prescription of a vial of pure Epi instead, which only costs about $20. The problem with the vial is that it is not portable, it does not include per-filled syringes, you need to actually inject someone using relatively sterile techniques, and you need to be conscious of needle hazards. A syringe, for convenience, may be per-filled, but will only hold for about a month before going bad. Also, syringes need to be filled exactly to 0.15 mL for children and 0.3 mL for adults.

Yes, the company decided to raise it's prices on the EpiPen, that's their prerogative, and yes, the FDA has blocked cheaper EpiPen alternatives from coming to market in the US before. This is because we're talking about a patented auto-injector, not the actual drug. If you can't afford the auto-injector it's not the end of the world, it just means you can save yourself hundreds of dollars a year by switching to a vial of Epi and taking a few extra precautionary steps. I agree, it's less convenient, but nobody is entitled to a fancy bells and whistles auto-injector.

Yes I'm pro pharma, I'm a pharmacy student after all. Look, I'm not saying there isn't greed and corruption in this industry, name on industry that is exempt from it, but it's largely over-hyped. It takes about 14 years and costs $1.2Billion to go from discovery to market, once on market you only have a patent for 7-12 years, and most drugs don't get past the FDA drug approval process, so it costs pharma corps BILLIONS of dollars to put a viable drug on the market and then they have very little time to turn a profit on it. It's just the cost and side-effect of a very stringent drug approval processes.
